summary: Superconducting transmon qubits are used to measure quasiparticle dynamics induced by particle impacts on a silicon substrate, establishing a statistical framework to extract the recombination rate $r$ and linear loss timescale $\tau_{ss}$ in aluminum films and reconstruct both deposited energy and interaction position. The measured recombination constants $r = 0.052$–$0.095$ ns$^{-1}$ and an unexpected correlation between $\tau_{ss}$ and deposited energy are validated against Monte Carlo simulation, demonstrating superconducting qubit arrays as energy-resolving particle detectors.
motivation: Quasiparticle poisoning from radiation-induced particle impacts degrades coherence across multiple qubits in large arrays, and understanding the underlying quasiparticle loss mechanisms (recombination versus trapping) is critical for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Five fixed-frequency transmon qubits on a $5 \times 5 \times 0.35$ mm$^3$ silicon substrate were monitored via time-resolved relaxation measurements during exposure to a $^{137}$Cs source ($\sim$10 mHz event rate). A binomial maximum likelihood fit to qubit relaxation waveforms was performed using a quasiparticle density model governed by the Rothwarf–Taylor equation, with $r$ and $\tau_{ss}$ extracted via an average pulse method and event-by-event energy reconstruction enabling spatial localization through phonon transport simulations.
result: Recombination rates were extracted with $r = 0.052$–$0.095$ ns$^{-1}$ (consistent with prior aluminum measurements), a linear correlation between $\tau_{ss}$ and deposited energy was revealed for $50\text{–}300$ eV, and reconstructed particle impact energy spectra from $137$Cs photons showed good agreement with Geant4 simulations (relative energy resolution $\sigma_E/E_{dep} \sim 10\%$ for $E_{dep} \sim 100$–$200$ eV).
